topIssues.title: op-service/txmgr: move test and dev L1s to Osaka, then delete the blob-proof path
topIssues.author: geoknee
topIssues.body:
txmgr chooses between blob proofs (sidecar v0) and cell proofs (v1, EIP-7594) by `CellProofTime`. The public L1s (mainnet, Sepolia, Hoodi) all activated Osaka in Oct–Dec 2025. The clients handle the two sidecar versions as follows:

- **reth, after Osaka:** rejects v0 sidecars (`UnexpectedEip4844SidecarAfterOsaka`).
- **go-ethereum, after Osaka:** converts v0 to v1 at `eth_sendRawTransaction`, but only for a transition period (`TODO: remove in go-ethereum v1.17.x`).
- **Both, before Osaka:** v1 transactions never get into a block. go-ethereum's block builder asks its pool for v0 transactions, and that pool holds v1 only. op-geth and reth reject v1 sidecars.

So the blob-proof path only serves pre-Osaka L1s, and today those are our own test and dev L1s.

## Plan

The test L1s move first, using only the existing cell-proof settings. The production changes then need no test churn.

1. [x] **#24186**: moves the op-e2e system blob tests to an Osaka L1. (Seb)
2. [x] **#24216**: test L1s to Osaka:
   - action tests and kona's Go proofs tests: default L1 at Osaka (`op-e2e/e2eutils/setup.go`), and the action batcher sends cell proofs by default
   - fork-transition tests (`dencun_fork`, `ecotone_fork`, kona `l1_blob_parameter_forks`, `l1_prague_fork`, `pectra_blob_schedule`): keep their pre-Osaka L1 segment, since nodes syncing from genesis still derive from Cancun- and Prague-era L1 blocks, but post blobs only from Osaka on
   - the op-deployer L1 dev genesis and the op-e2e system default L1 start at Osaka
   - every test txmgr sends cell proofs: `setuputils.NewTxMgrConfig` stops pinning `CellProofTime: math.MaxUint64`
   - the Prague Anvil op-deployer test posts no blobs, so it is out of scope
3. [x] **#24211**: txmgr sends cell proofs by default on every L1.
4. [ ] **#24213**: txmgr and txplan send cell proofs only, and `--txmgr.cell-proof-time` is deleted outright. It also deletes:
   - the action batcher's `EnableCellProofs` option
   - the action L1 miner's pre-Osaka sidecar check: it now requires Osaka for a blob transaction
   - what #24186 adds: `useCellProofs()`, the `CellProofTime` block in `e2esys/setup.go`, and `CreateEmptyBlobTx`'s `cellProofs` parameter
5. [ ] Confirm that no supported chain settles on a pre-Osaka L1.
6. [x] ~~**#24212**: delete the deprecated flag after a release.~~ #24213 deletes it outright.

Related: #24172.

topIssues.title: op-reth: pending block env uses parent.timestamp + 12 (L1 slot time) on OP chains
topIssues.author: sebastianst
topIssues.body:
## Summary

op-reth's `pending` block environment is dated `parent.timestamp + 12` — Ethereum's L1 slot time, inherited verbatim from upstream reth:

https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/68b009443f67cf830990e913bcbde8536cb15327/rust/op-reth/crates/evm/src/config.rs#L28-L39

On a 2-second OP chain that is up to **5 blocks / 10 seconds ahead** of the block the sequencer will actually produce, so `eth_call` / `eth_estimateGas` against `pending` can execute under a hardfork the real next block will not have activated.

## What is actually served today

**Without flashblocks: op-reth never builds a pending block from the txpool.** [`OpEthApi`'s `LoadPendingBlock` impl](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/68b009443f67cf830990e913bcbde8536cb15327/rust/op-reth/crates/rpc/src/eth/pending_block.rs#L66-L86) overrides `local_pending_block` to return the latest canonical header (with an explicit pointer to op-geth's `miner/worker.go`), and `local_pending_state` to return `None` — so upstream's `build_pool_pending_block` → `build_block` path, which would execute pooled transactions, is never reached. Pending *state* falls through to `state_by_block_id(Pending)`, i.e. the `newPayload`-not-yet-FCU block if one exists, else `latest`.

**With flashblocks** (`--flashblocks-url`, off by default) the pending block and pending state come from the flashblock overlay, and *that* block carries the sequencer's real timestamp via [`From<OpFlashblockPayloadBase> for OpNextBlockEnvAttributes`](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/68b009443f67cf830990e913bcbde8536cb15327/rust/op-reth/crates/evm/src/config.rs#L55-L66).

**But the EVM *env* is `+12` either way.** `eth_call` at `pending` gets its state from the flashblock overlay and its `CfgEnv`/`BlockEnv` from `pending_block_env_and_cfg()` → `build_pending_env(latest_header)`. The real next-block timestamp is sitting in `OpFlashblockPayloadBase` and is not used for the env. So flashblocks fix the state path and not the timestamp path.

**RPCs that consult the `+12` env:** `eth_call`, `eth_estimateGas`, `eth_createAccessList`, `debug_traceCall`, `trace_call`/`trace_callMany`, `eth_callBundle`, `mev_simBundle` — and **every** `eth_simulateV1` block at any base block id, because upstream computes `pending_env_attributes` before applying block overrides, so an explicit `time` override corrects `block_env.timestamp` but not the spec already chosen from `+12`. `eth_feeHistory` rewrites `pending` → `latest` first and `eth_gasPrice` never touches it; both are unaffected.

**Why the fork boundary matters, concretely.** The pending timestamp reaches [`spec_by_timestamp_after_bedrock`](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/68b009443f67cf830990e913bcbde8536cb15327/rust/alloy-op-evm/src/env.rs#L125), which picks the `OpSpecId`. That spec then drives [`L1BlockInfo::try_fetch`](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/68b009443f67cf830990e913bcbde8536cb15327/rust/op-revm/src/handler.rs#L150), which reads **different `L1Block` storage slots per fork** and selects a different L1-fee/operator-fee formula. Across an Isthmus or Jovian boundary a `pending` call reads the next fork's slots against pre-fork state. Base fee is largely immune (`OpChainSpec::next_block_base_fee` branches on the *parent* timestamp for the Holocene/Jovian paths).

Aside found while confirming this: `--rollup.compute-pending-block` is plumbed into `OpPayloadBuilder.compute_pending_block` and never read — `is_compute_pending_block()` has zero call sites. The override above unconditionally wins, so the flag is a no-op and should probably be removed or wired up.

## What op-geth does

op-geth **serves the head block as `pending`** on every OP chain by default — [`miner.Pending()`](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/op-geth/blob/v1.101702.3-rc.6/miner/miner.go#L167-L189):

```go
if miner.chainConfig.Optimism != nil && !miner.config.RollupComputePendingBlock {
    // For compatibility when not computing a pending block, we serve the latest block as "pending"
```

`RollupComputePendingBlock` defaults to false. This landed in [op-geth#93](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/op-geth/pull/93) ("miner,eth: latest block as pending block on rollup", merged 2023-05-26), for two reasons: not leaking txpool contents before the sequencer commits to them, and not paying to rebuild a pending block every 2 seconds. op-geth also skips upstream's nil-ing of `hash`/`nonce`/`miner` on OP chains, so `eth_getBlockByNumber("pending")` returns a real canonical block identical to `latest`.

**Consequence: op-geth has no timestamp to get wrong.** `pending` ≡ `latest`, so `eth_call` at `pending` executes under the head header — a real, past timestamp. There is no `+12` and no L2 block-time constant anywhere in that path. (The opt-in `--rollup.computependingblock` path uses `now()` floored at `parent.Time + 1`, inherited from upstream geth. Upstream go-ethereum itself still builds a pending block from the txpool and is actively maintaining that code.)

## Options

1. **Derive the timestamp from the chain's block time.** The EL has no block time: `OpChainSpec` is a single-field newtype over reth's `ChainSpec`, and neither has any notion of slot duration. The value *is* already inside the binary — `block_time = 2` ships in the embedded `res/superchain-configs.tar` — and is dropped by the 3-field [`ChainMetadata`](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/68b009443f67cf830990e913bcbde8536cb15327/rust/op-reth/crates/chainspec/src/superchain/chain_metadata.rs#L15-L19) deserializer. Plumbing it in means widening `ChainMetadata` → `ChainConfigExtraFields` → `From<Genesis> for OpChainSpec` → a field/accessor on `OpChainSpec`, then a custom `PendingEnvBuilder` (today `NextEnv = ()` dispatches to the chainspec-less `BuildPendingEnv`). Moderate, and it still leaves non-registry devnets uncovered without a CLI flag. kona's `RollupConfig.block_time` exists but op-reth has zero references to `RollupConfig`.
2. **`parent.timestamp + 1`.** One line. It is the lower bound of the next block's timestamp for every OP block time, so `pending` can never activate a fork ahead of the real next block. It under-approximates by `block_time - 1` seconds, which means `pending` behaves like `latest` w.r.t. forks — exactly what op-geth does. (`max(parent+1, now)` is worse: on a lagging or syncing node `now` overshoots arbitrarily.)
3. **Stop serving a locally built pending block.** Already the case — op-reth mirrors op-geth here. Nothing to do; the gap is only the env.

## Recommendation

**Option 2**, implemented in [#22691](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/pull/22691). It removes the L1 slot-time assumption, makes `pending` conservative in the direction that cannot execute under a not-yet-active fork, and matches what op-geth already returns. Option 1 remains the "right" long-term answer if `pending` should ever model the *actual* next block (and would also let flashblocks supply their real timestamp to the env) — worth a follow-up, but it is a chainspec-plumbing change, not a one-liner.

There are no tests and no TODOs on `build_pending_env` today; the fix adds a fork-boundary regression test.

🤖 *Co-created with Claude Fable 5*

topIssues.title: op-interop-mon: Alert when the ETHLiquidity balance is low
topIssues.author: ajsutton
topIssues.body:
`ETHLiquidity.mint` reverts if the contract does not have enough ETH. Then `relayETH` fails, and users' ETH stays stuck until an L2 hard fork refills the balance.

op-interop-mon must check the `ETHLiquidity` balance on each interop chain and alert when it is low. The check is in ethereum-optimism/optimism-premium#361. This issue tracks the merge and deployment of that check. ethereum-optimism/optimism#23804 tracks the expiry checks from the same PR.

Blocks launch.

Filed by Claude from the Lagoon interop FMA (FM13).

topIssues.title: op-service/txmgr: delete the deprecated --txmgr.cell-proof-time flag
topIssues.author: geoknee
topIssues.body:
After #24210, txmgr builds cell-proof sidecars only and ignores `--txmgr.cell-proof-time` (`*_TXMGR_CELL_PROOF_TIME`). The flag is hidden: setting it logs a warning, and a time in the future fails at startup, because that operator expects blob proofs.

Once a release of op-batcher, op-proposer and op-challenger has shipped with that warning, delete:

- the `txmgr.cell-proof-time` flag, `CellProofTimeFlagName`, and `CLIConfig.CellProofTime` in `op-service/txmgr/cli.go`
- the warning in `NewConfig`, the future-time check in `CLIConfig.Check`, and their tests

`opql` (`acceptance-tests/opqlnode/fusaka_test.go`) sets `CellProofTime`; it needs updating when it next bumps op-service.

topPRs.title: op-deployer,op-chain-ops!: run every deploy script on forge and delete the Go script host
topPRs.author: nonsense
topPRs.body:
This PR is split into a stack for review: #23663 → #23664 → #23665 → #23666 → #23667 → #23668 → #23669. The stack has later review fixes; this PR stays open as the CI-green reference.

op-deployer ran its deploy scripts on `op-chain-ops/script`, an in-process Go EVM. That host needs EVM hooks that only op-geth has (cheatcode precompiles, pranks, no code-size limit), so it blocks the move to upstream go-ethereum (#20266). After this PR, forge is the only script engine, and the Go host and `op-chain-ops/interopgen` are deleted.

**Effect on users**

- op-deployer runs forge for every deployment, and anvil for `prepare` and `continue`. It downloads the pinned Foundry release on Linux and macOS when the tools are not on PATH. The Docker images ship both.
- Genesis deployments (`apply --deployment-target genesis`, op-e2e, sysgo) run the scripts offline on forge. The L1 and L2 genesis output does not change: before the switch, a differential test found equal state roots from both engines on eight reference intents.
- Live `apply` and `bootstrap` broadcast with forge, one transaction at a time, and no longer through op-service's txmgr. As txmgr did, each transaction gets the node's gas estimate just before forge sends it, a tip of at least 1 gwei, and a fee cap of twice the base fee (at least 1 gwei) plus the tip. Unlike txmgr, forge does not bump the fee of, or resubmit, a stuck transaction. forge gets the deployer key in a temporary encrypted keystore that only the user can read, never on its command line.
- `prepare` and `continue` simulate the deployment on an ephemeral anvil fork of the L1, as the deployer, without its key. `continue` then checks the simulated transactions and replays them to L1 through txmgr.
- op-deployer never compiles. It refuses a contracts bundle that would make forge compile, or whose scripts have no `runWithBytes` entrypoint, and it stops forge as soon as forge starts to compile. So a bundle must come from the contracts release of the same op-deployer release: an `https://` or `file://` bundle of an earlier release is refused (`tag://` locators were already rejected). The default, `embedded`, works.
- A contracts bundle is a forge project, so op-deployer does not trust its `foundry.toml`: scripts run without the FFI cheatcode, with file access only to the artifacts and to op-deployer's state directory, and forge scripts and anvil inherit only the environment variables that they need (`verify-contract` keeps the full environment, for its API key). anvil listens on loopback without CORS.
- forge runs need the `lib/` sources of the bundle but no solc compiler. Each forge script loads every artifact of the project, about 1.3 GB, so forge runs take one of `GOMAXPROCS/2` slots per host.
- forge's output goes to stderr. A failed script reports its revert reason.
- Removed: the `calldata` and `noop` deployment targets, `op-deployer manage`, the `--use-forge` and `--forge-slow-broadcast` flags, the Windows release binaries and `DeploymentCalldata` in `state.json`. contracts-bedrock loses the `InteropMigration` script and `DummyCaller`.

**Reasons the diff does not show**

- Every forge run uses its own copy of the compile cache and its own broadcast directory, so that concurrent runs (devstack) do not interfere.
- Each broadcast sends one transaction at a time. Without `--slow`, forge waited forever when a node dropped one of several transactions that it sent at once.
- Bundle builds run one `forge script` to warm the script cache, as CI's `forge-build` already does. A single script's compile can choose other solc versions than the project build, and then forge compiles on the first run. The builds then check that a second run compiles nothing, and fail if it does.
- The interop harness and sysgo now run the interop migration on a live L1 through an EIP-7702 delegation from the ProxyAdmin owner, not in the genesis state. The L1 activates Prague at genesis for this.
- The test `RetryProxy` (op-service) now gives a client error (4xx, but not 429) to the client at once. forge calls methods such as `anvil_nodeInfo` that a proxyd endpoint answers with 403, and the proxy held each of these calls for about 40 s of retries, so the Sepolia tests of `init` timed out.
- sysgo waits for the L1 transaction index before it deploys: geth rejects receipt queries until its first indexing pass is done, and forge stops after a few quick retries.
- #23309 (genesis-output changes) is not in this PR, on purpose. It changes genesis output, which this PR must not do.
- CI jobs that run op-deployer from the checkout (op-e2e, sysgo, kona proof tests) now check out the contracts `lib/` submodules: forge reads the sources to check its compile cache, where the Go host read only artifact JSON.
- forge runs are not `--offline`: offline, forge requires every solc version of the cache installed even when it compiles nothing. Online, it resolves them from its built-in list and runs the cached artifacts.
- The `forge` package tests (anvil fork, compile stop, sandbox, environment, slots) run in CI only after #23643, which removes the package from the CI exclusion list.

**Review findings not fixed here**

- Live `apply`/`bootstrap` could keep txmgr by simulating on an anvil fork and replaying, as `continue` does. The #23300 plan chose `forge script --broadcast` for live deploys; this is a follow-up if fee bumping matters for these one-time deployments.
- The op-e2e interop harness and sysgo could share one `opcm.MigrateInput` type, and sysgo could check that its rollup configs and dependency set name the same chains, as interopgen did. Both are follow-ups.
- `opcm.NewForgeClient` takes no context for the forge download, and `opcm.PermissionedGameStartingAnchorRoot` now has only test users. Both are unchanged.
- Security review, not fixed: `continue` checks the sender, target, type and value of the call it replays, but not its calldata against the prepared input (that needs the script's encoding in Go); the RPC URL stays on the command line of forge and anvil, which have no environment binding for it; a crash during a broadcast can leave the encrypted keystore and its password file in a directory that only the user can read (forge refuses a password pipe); and a forge binary in the cache directory is trusted by its version.

Closes #23300, #23301, #23302, #23304, #23305, #23306, #23307 and #23308.

BREAKING CHANGE: The Go packages `op-chain-ops/script`, `op-chain-ops/interopgen`, `op-deployer/pkg/env`, `op-deployer/pkg/deployer/manage` and `op-deployer/pkg/deployer/upgrade` are removed. So are `opcm.Scripts`, the script-host `opcm` constructors, the `opcm.*ViaForge` functions (now `opcm.DeploySuperchain`, `opcm.DeployImplementations`, `opcm.DeployOPChain`, `opcm.DeployAltDA`, `opcm.DeployDisputeGame`, `opcm.DeployMIPS`, `opcm.DeployAlphabetVM`, `opcm.ReadImplementationAddresses` and `opcm.ReadSuperchainDeployment`, which take an `opcm.ForgeEnv`), `ApplyPipelineOpts.PrivateKey`, `UseForge` and `ReceiptQueryInterval`, and in `broadcaster` the `Broadcaster` interface, `CalldataBroadcaster`, `CaptureBroadcaster`, `NoopBroadcaster` and `BroadcastCreate2`. Go programs run Solidity scripts with forge, for example through op-deployer's `forge` package, take the upgrade input types from `opcm`, and build interop test worlds with an op-deployer intent. op-deployer users get forge and anvil from the release images, or let op-deployer download them. Users of `--use-forge`, `--forge-slow-broadcast`, or the `calldata` and `noop` targets drop them; forge is always used. Intents that point at an `https://` or `file://` bundle of an earlier contracts release use `embedded` instead. To move chains to interop, call `OPContractsManagerV2.migrate` as a delegatecall from the chains' ProxyAdmin owner, for example from a superchain-ops task.

topPRs.title: kona-peers,kona-disc,kona-gossip!: Keep confirmed peers in the bootstore
topPRs.author: aakoshh
topPRs.body:
### What

The bootstore records how each saved peer was confirmed, and a full store keeps the confirmed ones. Second PR of a stack for #23767, on top of #24155.

For operators:
- The file is `{"version": 1, "records": [...]}`, one record per node, with `udp_verified_at` (a discovery session that lasted five minutes) and `tcp_verified_at` (gossip dialed the node at its record's TCP address). Old files, a plain list, are read and rewritten.
- A full store evicts unconfirmed records first and peers gossip reached last, so sessions under fresh keys no longer push out peers that work.
- A public-only node no longer dials back a private node that started a session with it; the private node dials, and can redial. `kona_node_discovery_events{type="session_established"}` no longer counts those sessions.
- Saved records without a TCP address are no longer handed to gossip, which counted a dial error for each every minute.

BREAKING CHANGE: the bootstore file format changes; earlier kona-node versions fail on it at startup, so delete the file to go back. In kona-peers, `BootStore::open` returns only the store, `SkippedEntry` and `SkipReason` are gone, `valid_peers_with_chain_id` returns an iterator, and `BootStoreError` has a `NewerVersion` variant.

### Why

The bootstore saved every session's record, with nothing to tell a peer that worked from one that never did, and evicted the oldest when full. Anyone starting sessions under fresh keys could replace every saved peer, so that after a restart the node would bootstrap from the attacker's records.

### How

- Evidence is only what the node saw itself. A session counts once discv5 still holds it after five minutes, which means it answered a ping, much as geth saves a node only after several. A connection counts only if we dialed it: op-node dials from its listen port, so an inbound connection can come from the record's address without showing that we can reach it.
- Among unconfirmed sessions, the youngest is evicted first, as the attacker picks the rate of fresh ones. Ties are broken at random, not by node ID, which keys can be ground for.
- Dialing back without saving, from #23766, is reverted: a node that dials a record it doesn't save can never redial it, and its dial can leave the other node with only an inbound connection, which confirms nothing.

### Caveats

- The per-/24 limit on the store is deferred to #23764: one host with many keys can still fill it with records whose addresses work.
- Evidence uses wall-clock time, so a large clock jump can count a fresh session as lasted.
- Evidence doesn't expire yet; that's a later PR.

### Alternatives

- An invalid entry is skipped with `serde_with::VecSkipError` and logged with serde's error, rather than parsed entry by entry to log its content.
- Review agents run: `rust-code-reviewer` and `deletion-reviewer`; each fix has its own commit. Dismissed: the invalid-entry WARN not naming the file or the entry, moving gossip's private `tcp_socket` to kona-peers, and the Korean configuration page, left to the translation PRs. The general code review and security review skills weren't run.

### Potential follow-ups

- Seed discovery from the stored records, and hand gossip only confirmed ones (next PR).
- Expire evidence, once discovery has heard from the network after a restart.

🤖 Co-created with Claude Opus 5.5

topPRs.title: op-reth: warm the proofs-history page cache ahead of persistence
topPRs.author: jelias2
topPRs.body:
Stacked on #24055; this PR contains its commit too. Review only the commits after it.

The proofs-history engine persists on a single thread. It reads B-tree pages one at a time through mmap faults, so on network-attached disks it waits on one read of about 1 ms at a time. On op-mainnet hardware (n4-standard-16, Hyperdisk Balanced 20k IOPS) persisting a block waits on about 900 to 1,200 such reads and takes about 700 ms, while the disk runs far below its IOPS limit and the CPUs are idle. During heavy periods the engine cannot keep up and proofs fall behind the tip. This PR reads the same pages earlier, from parallel read-only transactions, so the persistence transaction finds them in the page cache.

Effect on operators: none by default. `--proofs-history.prefetch-threads N` (default 0, off; 0–64) enables warming:
- When a block enters the engine's buffer, the pages its write will touch are read.
- When a batch has been persisted, the pages the prunes of the next two batches will touch are read. Two batches, so that a prune's pages are read a whole batch before it runs.
- Warming only reads. Work that is dropped, late or failed costs performance, never correctness.

Measured on a pair of op-mainnet followers with production hardware (devnets-private#2562), with 8 threads. Each row compares the two nodes over the same blocks.

At the tip, persistence time per block:

| | control | with warming |
|---|---|---|
| first commit | 721 ms | 244 ms |
| second commit | 645 ms | 190 ms |
| second commit, ten minutes of heavier blocks (about twice the keys) | 1,354 ms | 323 ms |

In the second commit's 190 ms the write takes 25 ms, the prune 89 ms and the commit 76 ms; the control spends 110, 459 and 76 ms. The persistence thread waits on about 70 disk reads per block instead of about 790.

One node catching up, so that persistence was saturated, persisted 1.44 blocks per second before, 2.6 to 2.8 with the first commit and 2.7 with the second. The first commit left about 260 reads per block in the prune, because its prune pass started when the previous batch finished and scanned changesets on one thread. The second commit removed them (prune 280 to 80 ms per block), and the limit moved to the disk: at 2.7 blocks per second it runs at its provisioned 20,000 IOPS, with about 4,800 page writes and 1,300 reads per block, so commits wait on their writes (71 to 199 ms per block). Catching up also re-executes each block on the engine thread, which takes about 310 ms per block.

New metrics:
- `reth_optimism_trie_engine_prefetch_{write,prune}_duration_seconds` and `..._{write,prune}_keys_total`.
- `reth_optimism_trie_engine_prefetch_dropped_jobs_total`: block writes that were not warmed because warming fell behind persistence. `..._failed_jobs_total`: warming jobs that failed.
- `reth_optimism_trie_storage_phase_major_faults{operation,phase,table}` and `reth_optimism_trie_storage_write_state_major_faults`: major page faults on the persistence thread per phase, which are the disk reads it waited on. They are read from `/proc/thread-self/stat` and are `0` off Linux.

Choices the diff does not explain:
- The store receives the block diff and a block range, not key lists, so it derives the keys the way its own write and prune paths do. Tests compare the warmed keys with the keys those paths record.
- When warming falls behind, the queue drops the oldest buffered block and serves prune passes first. The oldest block is persisted soonest, so warming it helps least, and the prune is the larger share of persistence time.
- Each job spawns scoped threads instead of using a pool. A spawn costs microseconds against reads of about a millisecond, and the crate gets no new dependency.
- The live test marks each block as persisted by reth (the `Finish` checkpoint), because the pruner never prunes past reth's persisted head. Without that, no prune ran in the live tests.

Reviews: `rust-code-reviewer` ran on both commits. The second commit fixes its findings on the first: the queue policy under overload, the prune range arithmetic, a warming thread that a panic could end, the API shape, and missing tests. On the second commit it found no high-severity issue. Fixed from that review: blocks that stayed queued after an unwind or after a save completed outside the event loop (the queue now holds the buffer's blocks weakly), tests for the pass limit, a moved window and the completed-save hook, and smaller simplifications.

Dismissed, with the author's confirmation:
- A failure to spawn the warming thread panics at startup. The engine's two other service threads do the same, and one of them is spawned next.
- A save that completes while the engine waits for it (unwind, shutdown) does not request a prune pass. Each pass covers two batches, so the next completed save makes up for it.
- Blocks in the batch being saved are still warmed. A batch is written in order, so its later blocks still benefit.
- `spawn_with_thresholds` could be folded into `spawn_with_config`. It predates this PR, and the exex tests use it.
- The live test does not assert that warming ran. Unit tests assert each hook (`buffered_blocks_are_warmed`, `completed_saves_warm_the_next_prunes`, the prefetcher tests); the live test checks that persistence and pruning stay correct with warming on.

topPRs.title: op-core,op-chain-ops,op-node: pin golden vectors for the values only op-geth pins
topPRs.author: sebastianst
topPRs.body:
The op-geth differential tests are deleted at the cutover to upstream go-ethereum, and some op-core values lose their only pin with them. This pins those values as golden vectors while op-geth is still there to prove them. Test files only.

Every literal is op-geth's output, and this PR's CI proves it: the existing differential tests now run over the same case tables as the golden tests, or a new assertion compares op-geth's output with the literal. The op-geth half goes with the differential tests; the tables and literal assertions stay, and the files that stay use nothing that only op-geth provides.

Pinned:
- **Deposit transactions:** binary encoding, hash and JSON for nil mint, nil value, empty data, the system-tx flag and extreme values; JSON with a nonce and without the `isSystemTx` key.
- **Receipts:** trie preimage, binary and RLP encodings of deposit receipts before Regolith, before Canyon and after it, with and without logs; a post-exec receipt; the receipts root over a mixed list.
- **Fees:** `L1CostBedrock`, `L1CostFjord` (including a zero FastLZ size and large sizes with maximal scalars), and `TxRollupCostData` per transaction type, unsigned and signed.
- **DA footprint:** the constants, every error path of the scalar extraction, and the footprint for the transaction-type mix, extra deposits and boundary scalars.
- **Chain config and genesis:** the exact chain-config JSON (key set and order), decoding op-geth-written configs and genesis files with and without `osakaTime`, the genesis header hash per fork schedule and message-passer variant, the full genesis JSON, and `NewL2Genesis` per schedule.
- **Other encodings:** post-exec transaction JSON, receipt JSON including `l1FeeScalar`, and the span-batch fields of a post-exec transaction.

`TestFjordL1CostParity` now runs over the golden table instead of its previous parameter grid.

Stacked on #24184, whose `CalcDAFootprint` takes binary-encoded transactions: the DA footprint vectors hold deposits, which a go-ethereum transaction cannot hold after the cutover.

Part of #24172.

🤖 *Co-created with Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2*

topPRs.title: kona-node!: verify L1 RPC data against block headers
topPRs.author: joshklop
topPRs.body:
With an untrusted L1 RPC, kona-node checked only block hashes. A dishonest or buggy L1 RPC could drop batcher transactions or deposits from what derivation sees, or install an unsafe block signer of its choosing, without any error. Unless `--l1-trust-rpc` is set, the node now verifies what it reads through its shared L1 client against the block header, as op-node does: header hashes, block numbers, transactions and receipts roots, and an `eth_getProof` proof of the unsafe block signer.

Closes https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/protocol-team/issues/568
Closes https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/protocol-team/issues/582
Closes https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/protocol-team/issues/583

**Stack.** This is part 4 of 5, split out of #23829. Merge them in order:
1. #23846: delete `DerivationDelegateClient`
2. #23847: check sync-start L1 origins against the canonical chain
3. #23848: share one L1 client across the node
4. #23849: verify L1 RPC data against block headers ← this PR
5. #23850: resolve pipeline reset bases by hash

**Effect on operators**
- With `--l1-trust-rpc=false`, the default, the L1 RPC must serve `eth_getProof`, or the node fails to start. The README, the flag help and the operator docs now say so.
- The chain provider's cache metrics replace the `block_info_and_transactions` value of the `cache` label with `transactions`. The bundled dashboards are unaffected.
- The L1 watcher waits a full poll interval after each poll, so a slow L1 RPC is not polled again as soon as it answers.

Until the reset-by-hash PR above this one removes it, the pipeline reset's separate lookup by number goes through the same verification as every other lookup.

**For reviewers.** Each commit is self-contained and builds and passes on its own. Each `!` commit's message states what breaks and how to migrate. Read in this order:
- verification, from `1b33bce8ea` to `eca5df16df`, then `ae0ab3940b`;
- the review fixes, from `6ac3383d08`;
- the docs, `f6ed432cdc` and `d7b86a68ed`.

**Reviews.** On #23829, I ran `rust-code-reviewer`, `deletion-reviewer` and a security review of the L1 verification against op-node over these commits. Here they are unchanged, except that the reset lookup is routed through verification; `rust-code-reviewer` checked that change. I skipped `deposit-reviewer` and `derivation-batch-reviewer`, because nothing here changes how deposits or batches are decoded. Finding dismissed, with the author's agreement:
- **Two cleanups are left for later:** a shared `BlockInfo`-from-header constructor, and one helper for mapping a missing block to `None`.

Older gaps the reviews found are tracked in protocol-team: https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/protocol-team/issues/570, https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/protocol-team/issues/571 and https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/protocol-team/issues/572. The L2 provider's verification is https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/protocol-team/issues/569.

BREAKING CHANGE: This affects operators, dashboards and code that uses the `kona-providers-alloy` crate.
- **Operators:** without `--l1-trust-rpc`, the L1 RPC must serve `eth_getProof`.
- **Dashboards and alerts:** queries on the chain provider's cache metrics that filter on `cache="block_info_and_transactions"` must use `cache="transactions"`.
- **Rust API:** `AlloyChainProviderError` gains `HeaderHashMismatch`, `BlockNumberMismatch`, `TransactionsRootMismatch`, `ReceiptsRootMismatch` and `InvalidStorageProof`, and `EmptyRawReceiptsForNonEmptyBlock` loses its `transaction_count` field. `AlloyChainProvider::unsafe_block_signer` returns `Result<Address, AlloyChainProviderError>`. `AlloyChainProvider::latest_block_number` and `AlloyChainProvider::chain_id` are removed.

Each `!` commit's message gives the exact change and the migration.
